Mon = “mõ” (nasal), ma = “ma”, mes = “may”. Same for ton / ta / tes, son / sa / ses.
Before a feminine noun starting with a vowel, use “mon” (not “ma”), with liaison: mon amie = “mõ-na-MEE”, mon école = “mõ-nay-KOL”.
Leur and leurs sound the same, “lur”, but “leurs amis” has a liaison: “lur-za-MEE”.
EAU = “o”: gâteau = “ga-TO”, cadeau = “ka-DO”. The plural has a silent -x: gâteaux, cadeaux.
Œu as in “sœur”: vœu = “vuh”. “Faire un vœu” = “fehr ẽ VUH”.
As in English, the possessive comes BEFORE the noun and replaces the article: “mon livre” (my book), “ma maison” (my house).
Unlike English, the possessive agrees with the THING owned: “ma maison” (my house, feminine), “mon frère” (my brother), “mes amis” (my friends).
Before a FEMININE word starting with a vowel or silent h, ma / ta / sa become mon / ton / son, so that two vowels don’t clash: “mon amie” (my friend), “son école” (his / her school), not “ma amie”.
2. Son, sa, ses: his or her?
This is the biggest trap. In French, “son / sa / ses” do NOT show whether the owner is a man or a woman. They agree ONLY with the thing owned:
It’s his car. (voiture is feminine → sa)
It’s her brother. (frère is masculine → son)
English distinguishes “his” and “her”; French doesn’t. If you want to be clear in French, add “à lui / à elle”: “sa voiture à lui”.
“Leur” is for several owners: “les parents de Julien et leur maison” (Julien’s parents and their house).
3. Review: the three tenses of A1
Congratulations! You now have three tenses, enough to talk about any moment of your life:

Time words tell you which tense to choose:
hier, la semaine dernière, il y a trois mois
aujourd’hui, maintenant, en ce moment, depuis
demain, la semaine prochaine, dans trois jours
That’s exactly what Ioana does in the dialogue: “Il y a trois mois, je suis arrivée…” (past), “Aujourd’hui, vous êtes ma famille” (present), “Je ne vais pas dire mon vœu” (future).

In France you don’t say “Bon anniversaire” before the day: it’s considered bad luck. And a present is opened straight away, in front of the person who gave it.
“Joyeux anniversaire” is also the song (to the same tune as “Happy birthday”): “Joyeux anniversaire, joyeux anniversaire…”.

On the evening of her birthday, Ioana got home at midnight. She didn’t open Julien’s present straight away. First she took out her old notebook.
In this notebook she has written French words since she arrived. On the first page there’s only: “bonjour, merci, au revoir, je ne comprends pas”.
She reread the pages and smiled. In September she was afraid of everything: the phone, the baker, the meetings at the office.
She remembered her first day at Atelier Rhône. She didn’t understand Nathalie’s numbers. Ninety-seven! Today she counts to a hundred with no problem.
She thought of Sophie, who now speaks slowly for her, of Karim and his jokes, of Madame Bernard and her greedy cat.
She thought of Annecy, the turquoise lake, Brigitte’s tartiflette, the snow on the Semnoz. And of Julien’s hand, at the top.
In three months her life has changed a lot. She has a job, a flat, friends. Sometimes she even dreams in French!
Of course, she still makes mistakes. She mixes up “le” and “la”. She forgets the “ne” in negations. She says “je suis allé” instead of “je suis allée”.
But the French understand her. And she understands the French. That’s what matters.
On the last page of the notebook she wrote a new sentence: “Je suis heureuse ici.” Then she added: “L’année prochaine, je vais passer le DELF B1.”
Finally, she took Julien’s box. Her hands trembled a little. She opened the red paper, very slowly…
Victor, on the balcony, looked through the window. He already knows what’s in the box. But he’s not going to say anything.
